narrative.title: The short version.
narrative.highlight: I take complicated information and make it usable for the person across from me.
narrative.body:
That has been the job in every role I have held. A bank, an operations team, and an emergency room all ask for the same thing in different vocabulary.

At Goldman Sachs it meant reading 100 to 250 page loan agreements and giving clients a plain answer instead of a legal summary. At Vivint it meant finding a $2M gap inside operational data and building the case that moved executive resources toward it. In the ER it meant standing next to a physician during an emergency tracheotomy and knowing what came next without being told.

The other half of the job is trust. I do not push. I figure out what someone actually needs, I show up consistently, and I earn the right to ask. That is how a Spanish-speaking territory that previous reps had written off became one where more than half of new commitments came through referrals instead of cold outreach.

Analysis, clinical knowledge, and relationship building usually sit in three different people. I have spent my career using all three at once. Medical sales is the role that asks for all three.

startStories.title: The Territory Everyone Wrote Off
startStories.teaser: I was assigned a territory where the key stakeholder had already said no to reps before me, and the numbers showed it.
startStories.body:
My job was to find people willing to join our organization. Cold calling strangers rarely worked, warm referrals did. Most members weren't reps like me, they were local families who met multiple times a week. In each area, one key stakeholder connected reps to those members. Mine had shut out every rep before me, and the territory's numbers had suffered for it.

I didn't push. My companion and I got to know his wife first, no agenda, just showing up over time. Eventually she mentioned he missed playing pickup soccer. That was my opening. We organized a game. He came. We kept it going. He went from closed off to actively referring members and trusting us with his network.

That territory became one of the strongest in the district. More than half of our new commitments came through referrals rather than cold outreach.

What that taught me is a no isn't the end, it just means you haven't found the right angle yet. Trust can't be rushed. That's exactly what it takes with a physician who's already said no to reps before.

startStories.title: The Goldman Standard
startStories.teaser: At Goldman I managed multi million dollar loan portfolios where one missed detail in a hundred page contract meant real money and real trust on the line.
startStories.body:
I managed a portfolio of institutional clients across multi million dollar syndicated loan accounts. The contracts behind those loans ran 100 to 250 pages of dense legal language, and a rate change buried at one specific point in the contract could not be missed. I learned to read those contracts front to back so I'd catch a discrepancy before it ever reached a client.

When clients had questions I answered in plain terms, not legal speak, because their trust in me depended on actually understanding what I told them. I kept every deadline I gave a client, including working from a plane on Christmas Eve once, because the commitment mattered more than the inconvenience. When teammates were out I picked up their accounts too, so no client ever felt a gap in service.

I was the face of Goldman to those clients. That meant white glove service and 100% accuracy at the same time, no exceptions. I kept every account in my book and never had a single issue escalate.

That role taught me accuracy and warmth aren't a tradeoff. A client has to trust you're never wrong on the details and that you value their time as much as your own deadlines. That's exactly what a physician expects from a rep.

startStories.title: The Rooftop Trauma Night
startStories.teaser: Three months into my EMT program, an emergency air transport put me in a trauma bay with a team I'd never worked with before, and no time to think about it.
startStories.body:
I was three months into my EMT program, about 2am during a 12 hour overnight shift. It had already been an intense night. My mentor pulled me mid task and told me to follow two nurses immediately.

We ran to the rooftop helipad to receive an emergency air transport. The nurses taught me the protocol on the way up. We received the patient and raced him through the hospital into the trauma bay.

The surgeon came in. A couple of EMT students were in the room. He barked a command to cut the patient's clothes off with shears. I stepped forward immediately and started cutting while the surgeon performed what I later identified as an emergency tracheotomy. The nurses looked over their shoulders and told the other students who had frozen to follow my lead.

What that night taught me is you don't rise to the occasion, you fall to your level of preparation and instinct. The team that trusts its training moves together without anyone having to think twice, whether that's a trauma bay or a physician's office.

startStories.title: The $2M Nobody Asked Me To Find
startStories.teaser: I was hired to build reports. I ended up sizing a $2M revenue opportunity and selling it to people several levels above me.
startStories.body:
I joined Vivint without knowing SQL or the business intelligence tools the team ran on. I learned both and delivered executive-level reporting within 9 days of starting.

The dashboards I built were used by the COO and 6 department leaders, and the numbers in them were presented on C-suite quarterly earnings calls. Once I was in the data every day, I started noticing patterns nobody had asked me to look for. I identified 7 to 8 operational inefficiencies across field and operations performance.

Together they added up to roughly $2M in revenue opportunity. I built the case, sized it, and presented it to senior leadership. They reallocated resources based on it.

Nobody assigned that project. Finding it required understanding the business well enough to know what normal looked like, and then being willing to bring a problem to executives who had not asked about it. That is the difference between a rep who reports on a territory and one who fixes it.

startStories.title: 41,000 ZIP Codes
startStories.teaser: As an intern I built a national marketing heat map, then ran a 50-state analysis nobody assigned me.
startStories.body:
My job at 1-800 Contacts was recurring financial reporting for executive leadership. The reports were accurate, but they did not show leadership where their advertising money was actually working.

I built a nationwide marketing performance heat map covering more than 41,000 U.S. ZIP codes, so leadership could see advertising spend against customer acquisition geographically instead of in a spreadsheet. It exposed inefficient spend and highlighted markets worth growing.

Outside my assigned responsibilities I then ran an independent market analysis across all 50 states using a visualization approach the team had not used before. The team adopted it, and I trained all 10 analysts on the Excel tools behind it.

Data only matters when the person receiving it can see the decision inside it. Territory data works the same way. Numbers in a spreadsheet do not change behavior. A clear picture of where the opportunity actually is does.

startStories.title: 100 Advocates, One Certification Gap
startStories.teaser: I led a volunteer organization of 100+ child advocates where the problem was not recruiting people, it was getting them certified and active.
startStories.body:
As Executive Director of the BYU chapter of CASA, I directed a 5-member executive team overseeing more than 100 volunteer advocates supporting children involved in the court system.

The roster looked healthy on paper. The issue was that a meaningful share of advocates never finished certification, which meant they could not be assigned to a child. I focused the leadership team on completion rather than recruitment and drove up the share of active, fully certified advocates across the roster.

The role also meant working directly with judges, attorneys, families, and community partners, each with different priorities and no obligation to make my job easier.

Headcount is not performance and activity is not results. The number that matters is the one tied to the outcome, and getting there usually means coaching people through the step they have been avoiding.
